text.what: Catholic forms in lay hands, worked past the point the clergy sanctions. A tin leg pinned to a saint's robe; a jet fist tied on a newborn in the first week; a seed called deer's eye on a red cord; a Saint Christopher on the dashboard; a candle, a cleansing and a saint's image bought in the same market aisle as medicinal herbs. Nothing in the list is outside Catholicism's own vocabulary. What makes it a separate tradition is who decides where the line falls — and here the household decides, not the parish.
text.story:
The objects arrived with the ships and most of them are older than the crossing. Milagros — small metal or wax body parts offered at a shrine — are traced to the ancient Iberians of the Spanish coast, travelled with the Spanish into Central and South America, and still hold in rural Andalusia, Catalonia and Majorca alongside their American forms. Jet amulets have been cut since the Neolithic; by the end of the Middle Ages the working of jet religious objects was concentrated at Santiago de Compostela and sold to pilgrims on the Camino, and the Asturian fist for a baby went from there into the Spanish Caribbean. Edward Tabor traces that fist further back, to Muslim North Africa, citing Washington Irving's 1829 description of a comparable jet hand among the Moors of Barbary, into Spain during the Moorish period of 711 to 1492 and on to the colonies.

The local material entered the same kit. In Mexico the ojo de venado is a Mucuna seed; México Desconocido traces its career as an amulet to Xichú in northeastern Guanajuato and notes the plant also grew in Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla, San Luis Potosí and Veracruz, so other regions may have arrived at the use independently. Newborns get one against mal de ojo; adults take one up for a hard stretch; drivers hang one where they can see it.

The argument in this tradition is unusually well documented because the clergy write it down. The Catechism of the Catholic Church condemns attributing a magical importance to otherwise lawful practices and crediting an object's efficacy to its material form. The priest Eduardo Hayen Cuarón condemned the ojo de venado by name, as an amulet and therefore an esoteric practice, malign and the work of Satan. Set against that, a Saint Christopher medal sold in Spanish-speaking markets carries a printed promise — 'Si en San Cristóbal confías, de accidente no morirás', if you trust in Saint Christopher you will not die in an accident — which is exactly the proposition the Catechism warns against, printed on a devotional article and sold in a shop. Both facts are on the record. This atlas prints them side by side and settles nothing.

The markets are where the tradition is legible as a system. At the Mercado de Sonora in Mexico City, established with other public markets by the city government on 23 September 1957 to regulate retail trade, medicinal herbs and magical and occult goods occupy aisles at the back of a single metal-framed nave. The two categories are not separate, and the account says so. Candles, saints' images, cleansings and herbs are bought in the same visit, from the same stallholders, by customers across the income range. In Lima and La Paz the equivalent counters sell the same combination with Andean material alongside.

*Inference —* the tradition's defining move is a doubling rather than a substitution. A saint does not replace a charm and a charm does not replace a saint; the same object is both, and which one it is depends on who is asked. That is why this record sits beside catholic-sacramentals rather than inside it: the sacramental tradition is defined by the Church drawing a line, and this one by households drawing it somewhere else.
text.how: Bought rather than made, in a church, a cathedral, a churchyard stall, a botánica or a market aisle, and then put to work in a named place: pinned to a saint's image or a shrine wall, tied to an infant's wrist within days of birth, hung from a rear-view mirror, set on a home altar, carried in a pocket. Some are blessed by a priest and some are not, and the tradition does not treat that as the deciding fact. Milagros can be offered as a reminder of what the petitioner needs or in thanks for a prayer already answered, and the shape does the pointing — though the code is local, not universal, so a leg can mean a leg or a journey.
text.today: Live across Mexico, the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, the Andes, parts of the United States, and the Philippines by the same galleon route. Prices have been published for one object: Tabor gives US$3 to US$10 for an azabache in a botánica and US$9 to US$55 online at the time he wrote, in 2023, and reports that 29 per cent of the wearers he surveyed had chosen the fist and 71 per cent the polyhedron. Quiapo Church in Manila draws millions on 9 January and thousands every Friday, with the stalls outside selling the amulets alongside. The Mercado de Sonora still trades, in a building the city put up in 1957 and has maintained badly since.

text_th.what: รูปแบบของคาทอลิกในมือของฆราวาส ที่ใช้เลยขอบเขตที่นักบวชรับรอง ขาดีบุกที่กลัดไว้กับเสื้อคลุมของรูปนักบุญ กำปั้นเจ็ตที่ผูกให้ทารกแรกเกิดในสัปดาห์แรก เมล็ดพืชที่เรียกว่าตากวางร้อยด้ายแดง รูปนักบุญคริสโตเฟอร์บนคอนโซลหน้ารถ เทียน พิธีชำระล้าง และรูปนักบุญที่ซื้อในทางเดินตลาดเดียวกับสมุนไพรรักษาโรค ไม่มีสิ่งใดในรายการนี้อยู่นอกคำศัพท์ของคาทอลิกเอง สิ่งที่ทำให้มันเป็นธรรมเนียมแยกต่างหากคือใครเป็นผู้ตัดสินว่าเส้นแบ่งอยู่ตรงไหน — และที่นี่ ครัวเรือนเป็นผู้ตัดสิน ไม่ใช่โบสถ์ประจำตำบล

dating.label: from the Spanish arrival in the Americas to now
dating.note: from_year marks the Spanish arrival in Mesoamerica, which is when the cited account says the milagro custom accompanied the Spanish into Central and South America. It is a convention, not an event: the sources date the objects' Iberian ancestry far earlier — jet amulets from the Neolithic, the milagro to the ancient Iberians — and date no single American starting point.

object.made_by: workshops, market stallholders and small manufacturers; bought in churches and cathedrals, from street vendors, in botánicas and in market aisles. Blessing by a priest is available and is not the tradition's deciding fact.
object.note: There is no single object. The fields are the commonest cases across the Latin American records in this atlas.

against.who: Mexican and Caribbean households: a Mucuna seed called deer's eye against mal de ojo, and a jet fist tied on a newborn within days of birth
Puerto Rican, Cuban and Dominican parents, who told Edward Tabor the azabache is against the evil eye and with it diarrhoea, respiratory infections, deformities and above all sudden infant death
petitioners at shrines, who pin a milagro shaped like the afflicted part to a saint's image as a reminder of the need or in thanks for an answer
the medals themselves, which print the claim: 'Si en San Cristóbal confías, de accidente no morirás' — if you trust in Saint Christopher, you will not die in an accident
customers at the Mercado de Sonora, whose back aisles sell goods for magic and the occult alongside medicinal herbs, the two not kept separate
the same market's stock, which includes crosses of ocote wood for good luck and chains of garlic to turn evil away

kin.as: the tradition's public object — left at the shrine rather than carried home, and the one that decides which saint gets which limb

the same move in another Spanish colony — church forms taken up and worked by people outside the clergy, across the Pacific by the galleon route
the tradition it shares a counter with in La Paz and Lima, and the one whose January blessing the Church joins in on

the act most of these objects exist for, and the one the markets are laid out around

countries.note: Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Spain and the southern United States are named in the sources read here; Peru and Bolivia for the market counters; Guatemala is the weakest entry; the Philippines is included because the same galleon route carried the same doubling of saint and charm, which the quiapo-church record sets out
